text: Cavernous means huge and hollow inside — so big and so empty that a person standing in the middle of it looks small. The word is built out of cavern, another word for a cave, and it almost always describes an indoor space. Calling Strawberry Arena cavernous tells you that thousands of racers can run laps inside it with room to spare.

To concede is to admit that something is true even when it counts against you. You are not giving up the whole argument, just handing over one point of it, usually right before you make your own. Here the co-founder of Hyrox concedes that his races are expensive, and then argues that people keep signing up anyway.

Solitary means done alone, or standing alone with nothing else around it. It belongs to the same family as solo and solitude. The article uses it for exercise: most people train by themselves, so working out is a solitary pursuit, and Hyrox turns that alone-time into something people do side by side.

A craze is something that suddenly becomes wildly popular, usually for a short while. The word carries a hint that the excitement is a little out of proportion, and that it may fade. The headline calls Hyrox a fitness craze, then jokes that this one keeps running instead of dying out.

Something gruelling is exhausting and punishing, and goes on long enough to wear you down. A gruelling hike, a gruelling week of exams. Americans spell it grueling, with one l. The article calls Hyrox a gruelling mix of running and strength-training because racers keep working for roughly 90 minutes.

Strength-training is exercise meant to make muscles stronger rather than to keep you moving for a long time: lifting, pushing and pulling heavy things for a few seconds at a time. It is the opposite half of the pair from cardio, which is steady effort like running. Hyrox puts both halves in one race.

To work up a sweat is to exercise or labour hard enough that you start sweating. It is a normal way to say you put in real physical effort, not just a little. The deck says Hyrox has people working up a sweat, which the opening scene then shows literally.

Strawberry Arena is a very large indoor stadium in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden, used for football matches, concerts and big events like this race. Its name is the setup for the article's joke that a few of the racers are the colour of the fruit — meaning their faces have turned strawberry red from the effort.

A chisel is a tool for carving stone or wood, so calling a body chiselled means the muscles show sharp, clear edges, as if the shape had been carved. It is a compliment about how defined someone looks. Americans spell it chiseled. Here it tells you the racers are serious athletes, not casual gym-goers.

Puffing means breathing in short, hard bursts because you are out of breath. You puff after running up several flights of stairs. The word describes the sound as much as the breathing, and it opens the article by putting you in a room full of people gasping.

You probably know slick as smooth, or as clever in a slightly untrustworthy way. Here it has its plainer meaning: wet and shiny, with a film of liquid on the surface. Slick with sweat means the racers' skin is shining because it is covered in it.

Little wonder means no surprise there, and it points back at the reason you have just been given. A writer uses it to say the explanation is already obvious. The article says the racers are red-faced, and little wonder — the list of what they have just done follows immediately.

A kilometre is 1,000 metres, a little over half a mile. It is the standard distance unit in most of the world, and it is spelled kilometer in the United States. Each running leg of a Hyrox race is one kilometre, so a racer covers eight of them in total.

A ski-training machine, often called a ski erg, is a gym machine with two handles on a cord that you pull down hard, over and over. It copies the arm motion of cross-country skiing and works the back, arms and stomach. No snow is involved, and you stay in one spot.

Outside a gym, to lunge is to throw yourself forward suddenly, the way a goalkeeper lunges for a ball. Inside a gym it is the name of an exercise: you take a long step forward and bend both knees until the back knee nearly touches the floor, then push back up. That is the meaning here.

A burpee is a single exercise that packs several moves together: you drop into a squat, kick your feet back into a push-up position, jump them forward again and finish with a jump into the air. Doing many in a row raises your heart rate fast, which is why they turn up in fitness races.

A kettlebell is a heavy cast-iron ball with a thick handle on top, shaped a bit like a kettle. Because the weight hangs below your hand rather than sitting in line with it, carrying or swinging one makes the muscles around your stomach and back work to keep you steady.

This is not the kind of sled you ride down a snowy hill. In a gym, a sled is a low metal frame loaded with weights that you shove or drag across the floor. Pushing one is hard, slow work, and it is one of the strength stations in a Hyrox race.

To lob something is to throw it in a high, slow arc rather than straight and fast. You lob a ball over someone's head in tennis or basketball. The racers have lobbed a medicine ball, meaning they threw a heavy ball upward at a target on a wall.

A medicine ball has nothing to do with medicine. It is a weighted ball, roughly the size of a basketball but several times heavier, that people throw, catch or lift for exercise. The name is very old and stuck around long after the reason for it was forgotten.

Respectable usually describes a person who behaves properly. Attached to a number it means something different: good enough to be taken seriously, though not amazing. A respectable race time of about 90 minutes is the time an ordinary fit person would be pleased with, while the best racers finish in under an hour.

To strive is to try hard at something difficult over a stretch of time, not just to attempt it once. It suggests real struggle and effort. The article says the fittest racers strive to finish in under an hour, which is a target most people at the event will not reach.

A cross between two things is something that combines features of both. You might call a lime a cross between a lemon and something sweeter. Hyrox is described as a cross between a relay race and high-intensity interval training, which tells you roughly what it feels like before any of it is explained.

High-intensity interval training, often shortened to HIIT, is a way of exercising in bursts: you go as hard as you can for a short interval, rest or go easy for another, then repeat. The alternating is the whole point, because it lets you spend more total time at a hard effort than one long push would.

A portmanteau is a word built by squashing two other words together so the new one carries both meanings: breakfast plus lunch makes brunch, smoke plus fog makes smog. The name comes from an old French word for a case that opens into two halves. Hyrox is believed to be hybrid plus rock star.

A hybrid is a mix of two different kinds of thing, working as one. A hybrid car has both a petrol engine and an electric motor. In Hyrox the hybrid is the training itself: running and rowing on one side, lifting and pushing on the other, in a single event.

Cardio is short for cardiovascular, which means to do with the heart and blood vessels. Cardio exercise is anything you keep up for a long stretch — running, rowing, swimming — so that the heart beats faster and the lungs pull in more air. People use the word as a plain noun: doing cardio.

The prefix un- flips a word to its opposite, so the unathletic are people who are not sporty and do not much enjoy hard exercise. Putting the before it turns the description into a group: to the unathletic means to people like that. The article admits the whole thing sounds awful to them.

Something nauseating makes you feel sick to your stomach. It is often used loosely for anything so unpleasant that thinking about it turns you off. The article jokes that a list of eight exercises stacked on top of eight runs may sound nauseating if you are not the sporty type.

A mass-participation event is one that ordinary people enter in huge numbers, rather than one you only watch elite athletes do. City marathons and charity runs are the usual examples: thousands of people cover the same course on the same day. Hyrox claims to be the fastest-growing fitness event of that kind.

Watch this small word. Placed in front of a number, some does not mean a few — it means about, roughly. Some 650 people took part is a way of saying the true figure was close to 650 without promising it exactly.

As a noun, features are the parts or qualities of something. As a verb, used here, to feature means to include or offer as a main attraction. September alone features events in 12 cities means September has races in 12 different cities.

Your pulse is your heartbeat felt through the skin, so to set pulses racing is to get people excited. It is a set phrase used for anything thrilling, from a film trailer to a rumour. The article is having fun with it here, because in this case the excitement really does come with faster heartbeats.

Peloton is a company that sells exercise bikes and treadmills with a screen attached, so people can follow a live or recorded class at home. It is named after the French word for the main pack of riders in a cycling race. That such a company now offers Hyrox classes is evidence of how far the format has spread.

Firm usually means solid or steady. As a noun it means something else entirely: a business or company. A home-exercise firm is a company that sells home-exercise equipment. This meaning turns up constantly in news writing, so it is worth knowing.

Bracing normally describes cold, fresh air that wakes you up — a bracing morning at the beach. Here it is used with a price: a bracing 2,200 pounds means a figure so high that it makes you catch your breath, the way cold air does. It is a dry joke, not a compliment.

The symbol £ stands for pounds sterling, the money used in Britain, in the same way $ stands for dollars. One pound is worth more than one dollar, which is why the article follows £2,200 with $3,000 in brackets for readers who count in dollars.

An acolyte is a devoted follower of a person, a cause or an idea. The word started out meaning a helper in a religious service, and it still carries that flavour of belief. Calling the person who writes Hyrox is a lifestyle an acolyte gently suggests the enthusiasm has gone a bit far.

To proclaim is to announce something loudly and publicly, as though it matters a great deal. It is a much bigger word than says. The article picks it on purpose: someone posting that Hyrox is not just a race is treating a fitness event like a declaration of faith.

Hype is loud, excited attention around something, usually more attention than the thing has earned so far. A game or a film can have hype around it before anyone has tried it. The article asks where the hype for Hyrox comes from, and answers with the boom in gym culture.

A boom is not only a loud noise. It also means a fast, large increase in something — a boom in house prices, a baby boom. A boom in gym culture means far more people going to gyms and caring about training than before.

Pumping iron is an old, informal way of saying lifting weights. The iron is the metal the weights are made of. The phrase has been around since the 1970s and still shows up whenever someone wants a casual way to describe weight training.

The ending -ee marks the person something is being done to or for, as in employee or trainee. A trainee is someone learning a job while already doing it. A trainee accountant is training to become an accountant, and is not fully qualified yet.

Adrenalin is a chemical your body releases into the blood when you are excited, scared or competing. It makes your heart beat faster and sends more blood to your muscles, so you feel suddenly alert and full of energy. That surge is the adrenalin rush. Americans usually spell it adrenaline.

Foster has nothing to do with foster homes here. To foster something is to help it grow or encourage it to develop. Leaderboards foster friendly rivalry means that seeing everyone's times ranked makes people compete with each other in a good-natured way.

A rivalry is an ongoing competition between people or teams who each want to beat the other. It can be bitter or, as here, friendly — the kind where you push each other to improve. The word comes from rival, and it usually suggests the contest repeats rather than happening once.

Pursuit usually means chasing something: a car in pursuit of another. It has a second meaning that is easy to miss — an activity you spend your time on, especially for pleasure. A solitary pursuit is simply a hobby you do alone.

The stands are the rows of raised seating around a sports ground where spectators sit. The word is almost always plural. The article notes that friends can pay to watch from the stands, meaning they buy a seat and watch in comfort instead of racing.

In British English a holiday is a trip away or time off, what Americans call a vacation, not a single day like Thanksgiving. A mini-holiday is a short one, a few days rather than a few weeks. Racers fly somewhere for a Hyrox event and make a small trip out of it.

A shortage is a lack of something. Saying there is no shortage of a thing is a roundabout way of saying there is plenty of it. There is no shortage of new destinations means new race cities keep appearing faster than anyone can visit them.

An influencer is someone who has built a large following online and makes money from what they post, often through deals with companies. The word only came into wide use in the last fifteen years or so. Danny and Zoe Rae post about racing and travelling, which is how the article knows about their trips.

Recreation is what you do for enjoyment and rest, as opposed to work or duty. You can hear the word create inside it: the idea is that free time re-creates you. The couple combine races with recreation, meaning they add sightseeing and fun to a trip they were making anyway.

To aver is to state something firmly as the truth. It is a formal, slightly old-fashioned word, and journalists reach for it to avoid writing says over and over. Mr Rae avers means Mr Rae states, with confidence.

Accessible means easy to get to or easy to get into. Sometimes that is physical, as with a building. Here it means easy for anyone to take part in: the trainer calls Hyrox one of the most accessible sports she has been part of because you do not need years of skill to enter.

CrossFit is a branded style of gym workout, started in the United States, that mixes weightlifting, gymnastics and hard cardio, and holds its own competitions. It grew very popular in the 2010s. The article brings it up as the earlier craze that Hyrox is now compared with.

A peak is the highest point of a mountain, so to peak is to reach your highest point and then come down from it. Saying CrossFit peaked in popularity in the 2010s does not just mean it was popular then — it means that was its high point, and it has been less popular since.

A hobbyist is someone who does an activity for enjoyment rather than for a living. The ending -ist marks the person who does the thing, as in cyclist or pianist. Hyrox attracts retired professional athletes and hobbyists alike, which is another way of saying experts and ordinary people race together.

To run out of breath is to be so out of puff that you have to stop. Asked about a trend rather than a person, it means run out of momentum and fade away. The article's question, Will Hyrox run out of breath, is a pun: it is asking whether the fitness craze will die down.

To grumble is to complain in a low, muttering way, usually without expecting anything to change. It is milder than protest and less direct than argue. Some grumble that tickets are scarce means a number of people complain about it, quietly and often.

Scarce means there is not enough of something to go round, so it is hard to get. It is the word economists use when demand outruns supply. Tickets for Hyrox races are scarce because far more people want to enter than there are places.

Upwards of a number means that number or more, and usually hints at more. Tickets cost upwards of £150 means £150 is the floor, not the typical price. It is a useful phrase for giving a lower limit when the top end varies.

Moritz Fürste is a co-founder of Hyrox and, before that, a hockey player who won Olympic medals. The article mentions his past on purpose: a decorated athlete starting a mass-participation race is part of why the format was taken seriously so quickly.

To exceed something is to go beyond it or be greater than it. Demand is still far exceeding supply means the number of people who want to race is much larger than the number of places available. That gap is exactly why tickets are scarce and prices stay high.

Observe most often means to watch carefully. It has a second meaning used constantly in writing: to say something, especially a remark that points out a fact. He observes means he comments, and it tells you the speaker is making a point rather than answering a question.

Outside computers, a format is the shape and set-up of an event: what happens, in what order, and under what rules. The format of Hyrox is eight one-kilometre runs with an exercise station after each. Saying the format has room to grow means the event itself, not any file.

A cabin can be a small wooden hut in the woods, but on a ship it means a bedroom for passengers. That is the meaning here: a four-day cruise with tickets for a cabin starting at £2,200 is selling you a room on board, not a hut.
